The relationship between brain size and intelligence is a contested topic with conflicting research outcomes. On one hand, [d3] reports that meta-analyses of over 8,000 individuals found a significant positive correlation between brain volume and intelligence (correlation coefficients of 0.24–0.33), concluding that "overall bigger brain volume, when analyzed across multiple studies, is associated with higher intelligence." Similarly, [d5] found in the largest study of its kind (13,600+ individuals) that "there is a positive relationship between brain volume and performance on cognitive tests," though brain size explains only about 2% of variability in test performance, with 98% accounted for by other factors. On the other hand, [d6] directly states that "although the male brain is 10 percent larger than the female brain, it does not impact intelligence," and [d7] notes that "weight also has little correlation with intelligence," citing a 1999 McMaster University study showing Einstein's brain was actually smaller than average overall. [d4] adds further complexity, suggesting that "intelligence may depend on brain size in at least a superficial way" but that there is likely "a law of diminishing returns" to increasing intelligence by adding brain cells, with larger brains also incurring significant energy costs. Taken together, the evidence reflects genuinely conflicting research outcomes: a modest positive correlation exists in large population studies [d3][d5], but individual cases and sex-based comparisons challenge any simple "bigger brain equals smarter" conclusion [d6][d7].
